name: Raga Rock
about: Raga rock was a press tag before it was a style: coined in 1966 for the Byrds' 'Eight Miles High', it covered any rock record that borrowed the drones, modal scales and the sitar of Hindustani classical music. The Kinks had got there a year earlier with 'See My Friends', George Harrison put a sitar on 'Norwegian Wood', and Brian Jones on 'Paint It Black'; by 1967 the instrument was on half the records in London and Los Angeles. Ravi Shankar was the reluctant patron and his nephew Ananda Shankar the one Indian who answered back. The fad passed, but the drone stayed in rock's bloodstream, and Cornershop, Kula Shaker and the Brian Jonestown Massacre revived the idea with varying degrees of seriousness in the 1990s.

artists.name: The Beatles
artists.why: Harrison brought the sitar to pop

artists.name: The Rolling Stones
artists.why: Brian Jones's sitar on 'Paint It Black'

artists.name: Ravi Shankar
artists.why: the sitarist every rock star studied with

artists.name: The Incredible String Band
artists.why: Scottish folk with sitar and oud

albums.title: Revolver
albums.why: The sitar and tabla of 'Love You To' are Harrison's first full raga, and the tape loops of 'Tomorrow Never Knows' turned Indian drone into the sound of 1966.

albums.title: Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band
albums.why: 'Within You Without You', recorded with Asian Music Circle players and no other Beatle present, remains the most serious Indian piece on a pop record.

albums.title: Fifth Dimension
albums.why: 'Eight Miles High' took Coltrane and Shankar into the charts and got the phrase 'raga rock' coined; the rest is patchy but adventurous.

albums.title: Aftermath
albums.why: Brian Jones's sitar on 'Paint It Black' and dulcimer on 'Lady Jane' made the Stones' first all-original album their most exotic.

albums.title: Sunshine Superman
albums.why: Donovan's turn from folk to Mickie Most-produced psychedelia, with sitar on the title track and a general air of incense; a huge American hit.

albums.title: Mr. Fantasy
albums.why: Dave Mason's sitar on 'Paper Sun' and 'Hole in My Shoe' put Traffic at the centre of London's 1967 raga craze; still a loose, charming record.

albums.title: The 5000 Spirits or the Layers of the Onion
albums.why: Williamson and Heron with sitar, oud and gimbri on a Joe Boyd production that made Indian and North African textures part of British folk.

albums.title: A Beacon from Mars
albums.why: The Los Angeles Kaleidoscope's second record, with the twelve-minute title jam built on oud, violin and drone; the most convincing American raga rock.

albums.title: Wonderwall Music
albums.why: Harrison's film score, half recorded in Bombay with Indian classical players; the first solo Beatle album and an honest document of his obsession.

albums.title: Ananda Shankar
albums.why: Ravi's nephew covering 'Jumpin' Jack Flash' and 'Light My Fire' on sitar over Moog and fuzz; a Reprise one-off that became a crate-digger's standard.

albums.title: In Blissful Company
albums.why: A Notting Hill band mixing flute, sitar and Hindu devotional chant with heavy rock; John Barham's arrangements give the debut its grandeur.

albums.title: Younger Than Yesterday
albums.why: Crosby's 'Mind Gardens' and the tabla-tinted 'Why' keep the Indian thread running through the Byrds' most varied album.

albums.title: Face to Face
albums.why: Ray Davies's 'Fancy' is a one-chord drone that followed 'See My Friends' into Indian territory, on the Kinks' first great album of English character sketches.

albums.title: Raga Rock
albums.why: A World Pacific cash-in with Harihar Rao's sitar on instrumental covers of 'Eight Miles High' and 'Paint It Black'; charming period kitsch.

albums.title: Sitar Beat
albums.why: Session guitarist Big Jim Sullivan playing pop hits on sitar with a studio orchestra; a lounge curio that nonetheless documents the 1967 craze precisely.

albums.title: Lord Sitar
albums.why: Sullivan again, pseudonymous, covering the Beatles and the Monkees on sitar; a record whose sleeve has outlived its music.

albums.title: Contribution
albums.why: The Texan singer and sitarist's first A&M record, with 'Man Hole Covered Wagon' and a raga-tinged folk rock that Shankar himself had taught him.

albums.title: Magic Carpet
albums.why: Clem Alford's sitar and Alisha Sufit's voice on an acoustic British record that treated raga as the material rather than the decoration; a quiet cult classic.

albums.title: Shankar Family & Friends
albums.why: Ravi Shankar with Harrison, Ringo and Tom Scott on a Dark Horse record that moves from Indian pop to ballet; uneven but warm.

albums.title: When I Was Born for the 7th Time
albums.why: Tjinder Singh's Punjabi-Preston band folding sitar, Allen Ginsberg and 'Brimful of Asha' into indie rock's most convincing union with Indian music.

albums.title: K
albums.why: Crispian Mills's Britpop band chanting 'Govinda' and 'Tattva' over Hammond and sitar; derided at the time, but the most popular raga rock since 1967.

albums.title: Their Satanic Majesties' Second Request
albums.why: Anton Newcombe's sprawling tribute to 1967, with sitar and tabla throughout; the Brian Jonestown Massacre's most consistent record.

albums.title: Ananda Shankar and His Music
albums.why: Shankar's EMI India record, with 'Streets of Calcutta' and 'Dancing Drums' sampled endlessly since; sitar funk at its most cinematic.

albums.title: The Seven Seas
albums.why: Rishi Dhir's Montreal band placing sitar inside jangling psychedelic pop; the most faithful recent revival of the 1966 idea.

note: Raga rock was a tag more than a scene; this list covers the sitar-era records and the few later bands that took the idea seriously.
